paragraphs: In the winter of Long’an’s third year, a thin skin of ice formed beneath Ba Bridge.

As Chang’an’s eastern gate was about to close, an ox cart from Jiangling entered with the last of the twilight. Frost clung to its felt curtains. A bundle of dried mugwort had been tied beneath the shafts to keep the animal warm along the road; by the time they reached Guanzhong, muddy water had stained it black. A gate soldier lifted the curtain with his spear. Inside, a man sat beside a lacquered chest, a copy of the Zhuangzi spread across his knees, the cuffs of his robe worn and fraying.
“What do you trade in?”
“Jingzhou brocade.”
“Where is it?”
The man closed his book with the faintest smile. “The river tolls have eaten most of it. I shall sell what remains once I’m inside.”

Unconvinced, the garrison soldiers brought out the lacquered chest. There were indeed two bolts of silk inside, so fine they slid through the fingers. Beneath them lay old books, brushes, and an inkstone. The soldier searched to the bottom and found a seam. He tapped it with the back of his knife. It sounded hollow.
“Your name?”
“Yin Zhongwen.”

The soldier entered the name in the gate register and stamped his travel permit. An official collected the permit for inspection. As the cart rolled into Chang’an, half a chest of old books still lay concealed in a layer beneath its floor.

Winter nights in Chang’an were drier than those in Jiangling. Yin Zhongwen lodged at an inn in the southern market, where the proprietor set a brazier beside his bed. Before long the keeper himself came in to ask whether he wanted companions familiar with the accent of Jiangnan. Yin declined, but the account boards caught his eye: wooden slips recorded the guests’ names, native places, and number of nights, even their charcoal charges down to the last fraction. The keeper crossed the name of a merchant from the western peoples off one board and entered it on a debt-collection list, cursing a man who could speak handsomely enough but could not produce half a coin of what he owed.

Yin Zhongwen thought for a while beneath the lamp, then asked his attendant to fetch the lacquered chest from beneath the cart. When they broke it open, a secret compartment revealed a letter bearing no signature of Huan Xuan. Its silk edges had been pressed flat and neat, like a thin, sharp blade.

Before dawn the following day, someone from the Secretariat was waiting outside the Jingzhou guesthouse. The visitor came neither to arrest him nor to exchange courtesies. He asked only, “To whom does Master Yin intend to sell his brocade?”
Yin showed him half an uncut length of silk. “To anyone who will pay the price.”
“The Crown Prince has time for you today.”
“Then we shall see whether the Crown Prince can afford it.”

They looked at one another through the cold wind, and at last each laughed. As Yin climbed into his cart, the innkeeper was sweeping a dusting of snow from the threshold into the street. It occurred to him that the business he had come to Chang’an to conduct might be harder to sell than that half length of silk.

A charcoal fire burned in the Secretariat’s eastern hall, whose doors had been left slightly ajar. Fu Hong sat behind a long desk listening to two officials reconcile records of riverworks sent from Luoyang. Several counties along the river had been ordered to replace their wooden piles: seventeen hundred had been reported, but only twelve hundred had arrived. The county clerks claimed that floodwater had swept the rest away; the granary office had discovered that nearly three hundred had been resold for private gardens and ponds. Fu Hong ordered both sets of prices copied side by side for an inspection commissioner to check. Only then did he summon Yin Zhongwen.
“I hear you have brought brocade.”
“Only two bolts remain.”
“The looms of Chang’an have grown faster in recent years. If Jiangling brocade is too dear, you may have trouble selling it.”
“Then Your Highness is likely to find the other article I have brought even less to your liking.”

Yin presented the letter with both hands. Fu Hong read it without looking up at once. It offered commerce between Chang’an and Jingzhou and mutual nonaggression along the Han River. Should Huan Xuan enter and rule Jiankang, he might even send a son north and acknowledge the northern court’s calendar and legitimacy. Every sentence left a way out. Even the question of borders, the most important matter of all, was reduced to “the bounds formerly held, each preserved by its own side.”
“Your lord,” Fu Hong asked, “how much of a fleet does he now command?”
Yin gave the numbers of warships and granaries.
“Were those vessels built by the government of Jingzhou, or privately by the Huan family?”
“Your Highness asks very closely.”
“Then answer plainly.”
“Some were left by former administrations. Others the Huan family has built in recent years. All the sailors receive their pay from Lord Huan.”
“How did taxes paid by the people of Jingzhou become the Huan family’s pay?”
Yin glanced at the two sets of riverworks accounts lying on the desk. He had overheard some of the argument as he came in, and now understood where the Crown Prince’s questions began.

“Your Highness would find government ledgers in Jiangling too,” he said. “But Jiankang cannot command Jingzhou’s soldiers. Lord Huan can. Soldiers now recognize the hand that gives them grain. Books will not change that.”
“I asked where the grain comes from.”
“From the fields. From the rents and taxes the people of Jingzhou pay every year.”
“Then do not sell Jingzhou on their behalf.”

Yin Zhongwen’s hand stopped around his cup. He had expected Fu Hong to ask first whether Huan Xuan would restrain the Northern Garrison, or open the river routes if Qin marched south. Instead the Crown Prince had taken the letter all the way round and returned to the seemingly small question of who provided the food and who held the soldiers.
“Lord Huan has no intention of selling Jingzhou. He seeks an agreement under which the armies can cease fighting for a time.”
“If Huan Xuan loses to Jiankang, will this letter still bind him?”
“When neither victory nor defeat is decided, any peace must leave both sides room to maneuver.”
“And if he wins, Chang’an must acknowledge the Huan family as masters of the upper river?”
Yin refused to concede the point. Slowly he said, “At least someone governs Jingzhou today. That is better than leaving it without a master.”

Fu Hong folded the silk letter as before, ordered a cart to take his guest back to the inn, and said he might see the Heavenly King tomorrow. On his way out, Yin glanced back to find officials still bent over the riverworks books, copying out the entry for those three hundred missing wooden piles. Suddenly the secret letter that had been meant to dispose of the realm seemed to have lost its luster beneath a heap of wet timber.

Fu Jian coughed badly that night. Empress Gou urged him not to receive the visitor from Jingzhou, but he asked for a cotton-padded robe to wear beneath his ordinary clothes. He was no longer the Heavenly King who, a few winters before, could ride through the snow and mount the city walls. When his attendant fastened his belt, he drew the jade buckle in by one notch. Fu Jian touched the old hole, remembered the illness of the previous winter, and asked quietly, “Were the medicines sent from Luoyang shared among the sick soldiers?”
“They were distributed as ordered.”
He nodded before instructing them to admit Yin Zhongwen.

Besides Fu Rong and Fu Hong, only Quan Yi remained in the hall to take the record. After bowing, Yin Zhongwen let his eyes pass over Fu Jian’s graying temples. The northern emperor was thinner than rumor had led him to expect, and harder to read. Fu Jian invited him to sit, but his first question was, “What is the price of millet in Jiangling this year?”

Yin gave him a figure. Fu Rong immediately found the market quotations brought by traveling merchants; the two differed by twenty percent. Yin attributed the difference to expensive transport and soldiers’ levies along the way. Fu Jian listened, then ordered Quan Yi to record the discrepancy for use when they next discussed trade.
“Now you may speak of Huan Xuan.”

This time Yin did not begin by extolling Huan Xuan’s gifts. Jingzhou, he said, had long been mistrusted by Jiankang: whoever held the upper Yangtze would always alarm the lower reaches. Huan Xuan had defeated Yin Zhongkan and Yang Quanqi. If the court now tried to take his troops, a greater war was certain. Since Chang’an had no wish to renew the old campaign at the Fei River, why not agree with Jingzhou to leave one another in peace for the time being?
“Does Jiankang know you have come?” Fu Rong asked.
“No.”
“Then you still call yourselves ministers of Jin, yet come first to seek terms with an enemy state.”
“At times a minister’s loyalty consists in doing for his court what his court dares not do.”

Murong Chui had not accompanied the court into the hall this time. He was inspecting troops in Hedong, and even in his illness Fu Jian had not recalled him expressly for this interview. That was a relief to Yin. He had heard too many stories of the Murong family’s fallen kingdom, and feared having another man present to refute Huan Xuan with the history of his own life.

Fu Jian ordered a map spread out. The Han River was no more than a thin brushstroke on the silk, bending southeast from Xiangyang, passing Jiangling, and finally joining the Yangtze. Yin pointed out where Huan Xuan had river forts on either bank, and where merchants of the two sides might lower their sails. When they came to the country southwest of Jiangling, Fu Rong asked how many registered men there had yet to be drafted into the army. Yin’s answer was vague.
“You know the number of warships, but not who repairs their oars?” Fu Rong asked.

For a moment Yin had nothing to say. Then he lowered the hand with which he had been pointing at the map. “The Prince of Yangping asks about common households. I have brought only a letter. Lord Huan will attend to Jingzhou’s affairs himself.”
“Then I cannot grant him the standing he asks for in that letter,” Fu Jian said.
Yin looked up. “The Heavenly King does not wish to trade?”

“We can trade. We can also negotiate the river boundary. If your granaries run short after the autumn, bring a contract to Xiangyang and buy grain at the agreed price. But say no more of accepting our reign title or sending a son as hostage. I will not take Huan Xuan’s son, nor invest him with Jingzhou as a hereditary possession.”
“Lord Huan has never asked for a hereditary grant.”
“So much the better. Then whoever serves as governor of Jingzhou next year, I need not fear your claiming that Chang’an promised the province to the Huan family and its descendants.”
Yin understood the weight of those words. He rose and stood before the map, for the first time no longer pretending to be a merchant come to sell brocade.

“The Heavenly King speaks from Qin lands. Without Jingzhou’s troops, Lord Huan would not even have a road to Jiankang. The Qin court disarmed the private armies of the peoples of Guanzhong, but it could rely on the garrisons around its capital. If Jingzhou hands its army over to Jiankang, the Huan clan may not be able to defend even its ancestral graves.”

Fu Jian watched the narrow line of the Han River without answering. The envoy was not lying. Fu Jian himself had once relied on his own household troops to reclaim the throne. Had he first been forced to lay down his command, his name would not be heard in Chengming Hall today.

“Tell Huan Xuan this when you return,” he said at last. “He may send men to discuss the trading routes along the river. As for Jingzhou’s military command, let him keep hold of the forces he has now, and then consider how they might be settled in years to come. He need not trust Chang’an, nor must he begin by trusting Jiankang. But if he trusts only the single army in his own hands, sooner or later someone will command more soldiers than he does.”
Yin asked, “And to whom will the Heavenly King leave the realm behind him?”

Fu Hong’s expression changed slightly at the question. Yin did not withdraw it. Pointing toward the Crown Prince, he continued with undiminished courtesy, “If generals cannot hold their commands in perpetuity, and provinces cannot belong forever to one family, by what right may the Huans possess Jingzhou, and by what right may the Fus hand down all under heaven?”
The charcoal cracked in the brazier. Quan Yi’s brush stopped above the paper.

Fu Jian looked toward Fu Hong, and suddenly remembered Wang Meng’s hands, drained of color, upon his sickbed. In that year Wang Meng too had asked by what right Fu Jian should unify the realm. He had had answers enough then, but could not find the one he needed now.

“The Fu family succeeds to the throne by ancestral law, and by the deliberation of the ministers who serve today,” Fu Jian replied. “That is no argument for an unchanging right through ten thousand generations. If you mean to mock me for it, I can bear your mockery. But Huan Xuan cannot demand that I commit a wrong on his behalf merely because I have not yet solved every difficulty under heaven.”

At last Yin’s face betrayed something. He made no further argument, but bowed and asked leave to depart. Fu Jian ordered a written reply delivered to him. It dealt only with commercial routes and the stations of border garrisons; it promised no cession of territory.
Three days later the ox cart crossed Ba Bridge once more. The gate soldier recognized Yin Zhongwen and called out with a grin, “How did the brocade sell?”
“Only half a length.”
“Then you lost money?”
“Not necessarily.”

After leaving Chang’an, Yin opened Fu Jian’s reply in the cart. The paper was thick, the handwriting beginning to tremble. At the end was a seal of the inner court, not the imperial seal used for a formal investiture. He put it back beneath the chest’s false bottom, calculating how Huan Xuan would regard him when he read it. He had secured no princely title for his master, but he was bringing back a trade route that might stretch farther than a fleet could sail. Plainly Huan Xuan had wanted more.

On the day of his return to Jiangling, ships were drilling on the river. Huan Xuan listened to his account and was silent for a long while. Then he asked Yin to describe the official registers of Chang’an, its market prices, and all he had seen along the way. Yin had prepared an elaborate speech, but could only answer him point by point. In the southern market, he said, Xianbei merchants kept shops, and Qiang men pleaded lawsuits in Chinese characters. Old clerks at a crossroads had argued until dusk over three hundred wooden piles. Fu Jian was aging and coughed if he sat too long, yet had firmly rejected the notion of a hereditary Jingzhou for the Huan family.
“Does he truly care so much who owns a single province?” Huan Xuan asked.
“He does.”
“He may have persuaded the Murongs to relinquish Yan. I am not obliged to relinquish Jingzhou.”

Yin said nothing. Huan Xuan rose and pushed open the window. The winter wind blew in from the river, carrying the damp scent of reeds. He watched the standards of his fleet rise one after another into the wind. The overlapping hulls blocked half the breadth of the river. The grain, corvée labor, and trading routes of the hundreds of thousands within the city lay, at this moment, behind those crowded sails.
“Write me a proclamation addressed to Jiankang,” Huan Xuan said. “Say that I borrow no troops from the north and have not sold one span of Jingzhou soil.”
“Chang’an never agreed to an alliance in the first place.”
“The people of Jiangnan need not know how many terms we discussed.”
Yin studied his master. He had always thought himself adept at paving the road for armies with words. Now he discovered that a letter whose bargain had failed could become a weapon just as well.

Clerks in Jiangling were still grinding ink far into the night. Once the new proclamation was issued, Huan Xuan’s reputation as defender of the southern lands grew stronger. In faraway Chang’an, Fu Hong received a copy and placed it in the same chest as Yin’s secret letter. The writing on the two sheets differed utterly, yet both had come from the same affair.

Outside Chang’an the Ba River thawed, and the old bridge piles submerged through winter emerged one by one. Boats continued to travel up and down its waters. Some men sold Jingzhou brocade, others Guanzhong millet. By the time spring warmed the country, even merchants dispatched by Huan Xuan had arrived in Xiangyang bearing valid travel permits.
